learningObjectives.title: Sunspots, solar cycle and solar activity

questions.q: In which region of the Sun does nuclear fusion take place?
questions.explain: The extreme temperature and pressure in the core allow hydrogen nuclei to fuse into helium.

questions.q: What is the name of the visible surface of the Sun?
questions.explain: The photosphere is the visible 'surface' layer from which the Sun's light is emitted.

questions.q: Which process releases the Sun's energy in its core?
options: Hydrogen nuclei fusing together to form helium
Burning of hydrogen gas in oxygen
questions.explain: Nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium releases enormous amounts of energy in the core.

questions.q: Which outer layer of the Sun's atmosphere is visible as a faint halo during a total solar eclipse?
questions.explain: The corona is the Sun's tenuous outer atmosphere, only easily seen when the photosphere is blocked during totality.

questions.q: How is energy mainly transferred through the convective zone of the Sun?
options: By convection currents of hot plasma
questions.explain: In the convective zone hot plasma rises and cooler plasma sinks, carrying energy by convection.

questions.q: Approximately what is the temperature of the Sun's photosphere?
questions.explain: The photosphere has a temperature of roughly 5500 °C (about 5800 K).

questions.q: Which layer lies directly between the Sun's core and its convective zone?
questions.explain: Energy from the core first passes outward through the radiative zone before reaching the convective zone.

questions.q: Why do sunspots appear darker than the rest of the photosphere?
options: They are cooler than the surrounding photosphere
They are made of dark solid rock
They are holes right through the Sun
questions.explain: Sunspots are cooler regions, so they emit less light and appear dark against the brighter photosphere.

questions.q: Approximately how long is one complete solar cycle?
questions.explain: The number of sunspots rises and falls over a solar cycle of roughly 11 years.

questions.q: What is the darker, central region of a sunspot called?
questions.explain: A sunspot has a dark central umbra surrounded by a lighter penumbra.

questions.q: What is meant by 'solar maximum' during the solar cycle?
options: The time of greatest sunspot activity
The time when the Sun is closest to Earth
The moment of a total solar eclipse
The time when the Sun stops rotating
questions.explain: Solar maximum is the part of the cycle when sunspot numbers and solar activity are at their highest.

questions.q: Aurorae (such as the Northern Lights) are mainly caused by which of the following?
options: Charged particles from the solar wind reaching Earth
Meteors burning up in the atmosphere
questions.explain: Charged particles from the solar wind interact with Earth's magnetic field and atmosphere to produce aurorae.

questions.q: Why do sunspots appear to move steadily across the Sun's disc over several days?
options: Because the Sun rotates on its axis
Because the Earth is orbiting the Sun
Because the sunspots are drifting away into space
Because the Moon is passing in front of the Sun
questions.explain: As the Sun rotates, features such as sunspots are carried across the visible face of the Sun.

questions.q: A period of solar maximum occurs in 2014. Using the average length of the solar cycle, roughly when would the next solar maximum be expected?
questions.explain: Successive solar maxima are about 11 years apart, so 2014 + 11 gives roughly 2025.

questions.q: Which of the following is the correct rule when observing the Sun?
options: Never look directly at the Sun through a telescope or binoculars
Look at the Sun through binoculars for only a few seconds
Use ordinary sunglasses to look straight at the Sun
Stare at the Sun with the naked eye at midday
questions.explain: Telescopes and binoculars focus intense sunlight that can instantly and permanently damage the eye.

questions.q: How does the projection method allow the Sun to be observed safely?
options: The telescope projects the Sun's image onto a white card or screen to view
It uses a special mirror to look straight at the Sun
It dims the Sun using ordinary sunglasses at the eyepiece
It photographs the Sun so you never need equipment
questions.explain: With projection you view the image cast onto a screen, so no concentrated sunlight enters the eye.

questions.q: An astronomer wants to view the Sun's disc directly through a telescope. Where should a proper solar filter be fitted?
options: Over the front (objective) end of the telescope
Inside the focuser as a coloured glass
questions.explain: A certified solar filter must cover the front aperture so sunlight is reduced before it is concentrated.

questions.q: Why should a filter never be placed at the eyepiece end of a telescope pointed at the Sun?
options: The concentrated sunlight can heat and crack the filter, risking eye damage
It makes the image too dim to see
It stops the telescope from focusing
It reflects light back towards the Sun
questions.explain: By the eyepiece the sunlight is already focused, so it can overheat and shatter the filter and injure the eye.

questions.q: A student suggests looking straight at the Sun through ordinary sunglasses to watch a sunspot. What is the best response?
options: This is unsafe; sunglasses do not block enough harmful radiation
It is fine because sunglasses darken the Sun enough
It is safe as long as it is only for a minute
It is safe if two pairs of sunglasses are worn
questions.explain: Ordinary sunglasses do not reduce the Sun's intensity enough and can still allow serious eye damage.

questions.q: A sunspot has a temperature of about 4000 K while the surrounding photosphere is about 5800 K. What does this explain about the sunspot?
options: Being cooler, it emits less light and so looks dark against the photosphere
Being hotter, it emits more light and so looks bright
It emits the same light as its surroundings
Its temperature has no effect on its appearance
questions.explain: A cooler region radiates less visible light, so the sunspot appears dark compared with the hotter photosphere.
